questions.q: Which three rough dimensions does Salesforce's own guidance use to describe LDV-scale deployments?
options: Number of custom fields, number of validation rules, and number of page layouts
Number of Apex triggers, number of flows, and number of installed packages
Tens of thousands of users, tens of millions of records in a single object, or hundreds of gigabytes of record storage
Org edition, time zone, and currency setting
questions.explain: Salesforce frames LDV-scale deployments loosely around user count, record count in a single object, and total storage — used together, not any single measure in isolation.

questions.q: A dashboard is slow because a report is scoped to one territory that happens to own a disproportionate share of an object's records. Which LDV dimension is primarily driving this symptom?
options: Ownership/user concentration dimension
Storage dimension (large attachments)
Apex CPU time limit
API call limit
questions.explain: This is a skew-style, ownership-concentration problem rather than a raw record-count or storage problem — the report is slow because of how unevenly records are owned, not because of total volume.

questions.q: Why does this lesson argue that LDV status should be assessed per object rather than for an entire org?
options: Because Salesforce bills storage separately per object
Because only custom objects can ever experience LDV symptoms
Because standard objects are immune to data skew by platform design
Because a large org can have one object firmly in LDV territory while most of its other objects never trigger any LDV behaviors, so a single org-wide answer hides the real risk
questions.explain: LDV risk is a property of a specific object's volume, shape, and ownership pattern — a org can be mostly unremarkable while one object (like a high-volume transaction log) is deep in LDV territory, so per-object assessment is the only way to find the real risk.

questions.q: According to this lesson, what's the right planning question for a brand-new object with a modest launch-day record count?
options: Whether the object's name fits Salesforce naming conventions
What the object's growth trajectory is, and which LDV dimension (record count, storage, ownership concentration) it will hit first
Whether the object should be renamed to avoid confusion with a standard object
How many validation rules the object will eventually need
questions.explain: Because LDV problems are late-arriving and dimension-specific, the useful planning question is about trajectory and which dimension will bite first — not the record count the object happens to start with at launch.

questions.q: A custom object is designed to log every integration event, starting with only a few thousand records in its first month live. Why does this lesson say it still needs LDV-aware design decisions from day one?
options: Because any object with "log" in its name automatically qualifies as a Big Object
Because log objects are not allowed to use lookup relationships under any circumstances
Because an object remediated for LDV only after it already carries millions of production records faces much worse constraints than one designed with its trajectory in mind up front
Because Salesforce automatically deletes log objects that grow too fast without warning
questions.explain: An object's small launch-day count doesn't reflect its growth trajectory — a logging object designed to record every event is exactly the kind of object that will outgrow a naive design, and fixing that after the fact against live production data and dependent automation is far harder than designing it correctly from the start.
